EXEMPT SALARY THRESHOLD CHECKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Does this salary clear the overtime-exemption threshold?

The federal FLSA white-collar exemption salary threshold is $684/week — but California, Washington, Maine, Alaska, and New York all set a higher figure that controls instead whenever an employee works there. This tool checks a weekly salary against whichever figure actually applies, including New York's carve-out for the professional exemption.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Where the employee works, and which exemption

New York's higher figures apply only to the executive and administrative exemptions — the professional exemption uses the federal figure even in New York. Every other modeled state applies its higher figure to all three EAP categories alike.

2. The salary

Paid a fixed annual salary instead? Divide by 52 to get the weekly figure this tool compares — the result below also shows the annual equivalent of the applicable threshold.

Choose a state and exemption category, enter the weekly salary, then click Check.

Result

What this does not cover

  • Not a full exemption determination. This checks only the salary-level threshold — not the salary-basis test (whether pay is actually reduced for partial-day absences or variable work) or the duties test (whether the job's actual responsibilities qualify as executive, administrative, or professional work).
  • No computer-employee exemption. The separate federal computer-employee exemption ($27.63/hour as an alternative to the salary test) and any state-specific computer-employee rule are not modeled here.
  • Five states only. Other states may set their own thresholds this tool does not track; if the employee's state is not listed, confirm separately whether that state sets its own figure.
  • Point-in-time figures. These are the 2026 figures as published; a state's threshold can change again in a future year, and Alaska's figure does not take effect until 2026-07-01.

Common questions

What is the FLSA white-collar exempt salary threshold for 2026?

The federal threshold is $684/week ($35,568/year). The 2024 rule that would have raised it to $1,128/week was vacated by a federal court, and the Department of Labor's May 2026 technical amendment formally confirmed $684 as the operative figure rather than raising it.

Which states have a higher exempt salary threshold than the federal figure?

Five states, all effective 2026: California ($1,352/week), Washington ($1,541.70/week), Maine ($871.16/week), New York ($1,275/week in NYC and Nassau, Suffolk, and Westchester counties, or $1,199.10/week elsewhere in the state), and Alaska ($1,120/week, but not effective until July 1, 2026). An employer must meet whichever of the federal or state figure is higher.

Does New York's higher threshold apply to every exemption category?

No. New York's higher figures apply only to the executive and administrative exemptions. New York sets no state-specific threshold for the professional exemption, so the federal $684/week figure governs a professional-exemption classification even in New York — the detail this tool exists to catch, since every other modeled state uses one figure across all three EAP categories.

If a salary meets the threshold, is the employee definitely exempt?

No. Meeting the salary threshold is necessary but not sufficient. The employee must also be paid on a true salary basis (not reduced for partial-day absences or variations in the amount of work) and must actually perform exempt duties under the executive, administrative, or professional duties test. This tool checks only the salary-level test.

Is this legal advice?

No. This tool applies published federal and state salary-threshold figures to the numbers you enter. It does not evaluate job duties, salary basis, or any other element of an exemption determination, and it is not a substitute for reviewing current DOL and state guidance or consulting a qualified employment attorney or HR compliance professional before classifying an employee.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified employment attorney or HR compliance professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming an employee's full exemption status before classifying them. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (threshold_checked, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Checking whether a tip pool is FLSA-eligible instead? The tip pool compliance calculator is the one for that — a different FLSA wage-and-hour figure, tip credit eligibility rather than the exempt salary minimum.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This checker vs. checking the FLSA salary threshold yourself

Checking a salary against the FLSA white-collar exemption threshold looks like comparing one number to another. It is, once you have the right number -- but which number applies depends on the employee's work state, and in one state, on the exemption category too. A manual check that reaches for a single figure and applies it everywhere gets exactly the case that differs wrong.

Where a manual check usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake checking it by handWhat this checker does
Picking the right threshold for the stateApplying the federal $684/week figure to every employee, missing that California, Washington, Maine, Alaska, and New York each set a higher figure that controls instead for an employee working there.Applies the federal figure or the applicable state figure, whichever is higher, based on the state you select.
New York's category-specific carve-outApplying New York's higher regional figure to every exemption category, when it applies only to the executive and administrative exemptions -- a professional-exemption classification in New York is governed by the federal $684/week figure instead.Applies New York's higher figure only to the executive and administrative categories, and the federal figure to the professional category, automatically.
State effective datesApplying a state's higher 2026 figure before it actually takes effect -- Alaska's $1,120/week figure is not effective until July 1, 2026, unlike the other four states' January 1, 2026 dates.States each figure's effective date alongside the result, so a check run before that date isn't silently overclaiming it.
Treating "meets the threshold" as "is exempt"Stopping at the salary comparison and classifying the employee exempt on that basis alone.States every time that the salary threshold is necessary, not sufficient -- the salary-basis and duties tests still apply and are not checked here.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The checker runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is sent to a server.

Worked example: the same salary and location, two exemption categories

This is the checker's own shipped "load an example" scenario -- open the checker and click it to see the same numbers.

EmployeeApplicable thresholdMeets it?
$900/week, professional exemption, NYC area$684.00/week (federal -- New York sets no professional-specific figure)Yes
$900/week, administrative exemption, NYC area$1,275.00/week (New York's downstate figure)No -- $375.00 short

Same salary, same office. A manual check that learned "the New York figure is $1,275/week" from the first case and applied it to every category would have wrongly failed the professional employee, or one that learned "$900 clears the threshold here" from the professional case and applied it to the administrative employee would have wrongly passed them. Both mistakes run in this checker's worked example, in opposite directions, from the same starting fact.

Common questions

If a salary clears the federal $684/week threshold, is that always enough?

No -- only in a state that has not set its own higher figure. Five states currently have: California, Washington, Maine, Alaska, and New York. An employee paid well above $684/week can still fail the applicable threshold if they work in one of those states and the state figure is higher, which is the single most common way a manual check that only knows the federal number gets the answer wrong.

Does New York's higher salary threshold apply to every exemption category?

No, and this is the detail most likely to be missed by hand. New York's higher regional figures ($1,275/week in NYC and Nassau/Suffolk/Westchester, $1,199.10/week elsewhere in the state) apply only to the executive and administrative exemptions. New York sets no separate threshold for the professional exemption, so the federal $684/week figure governs a professional-exemption classification even in New York -- while an executive or administrative employee at the identical salary and location is judged against the much higher state figure.

Why would the same weekly salary pass for one employee and fail for another at the identical company location?

Because the applicable threshold depends on the exemption category, not just the state. A $900/week employee in the NYC area classified under the professional exemption meets the threshold -- the federal $684/week figure governs, since New York sets no professional-specific figure. A $900/week employee at the same company, same location, classified under the administrative exemption instead does not meet the threshold: New York's $1,275/week figure applies to that category, and $900 is $375 short.

Does every state's higher threshold take effect on the same date?

No. California, Washington, Maine, and New York's 2026 figures are effective January 1, 2026, but Alaska's $1,120/week figure does not take effect until July 1, 2026 -- a manual check applied before that date should still use the federal $684/week figure for an Alaska employee, not the higher figure that has not taken effect yet.

If a salary meets the applicable threshold, does that make the employee exempt?

No. The salary threshold is a necessary condition, never a sufficient one. The employee must also be paid on a true salary basis (not reducible for partial-day absences or variations in the quantity of work performed) and must actually perform exempt duties under the executive, administrative, or professional duties test. This tool checks only the salary-level half of the test.

No warranty. This page and the linked checker apply published federal and state figures to numbers you supply. They are not legal, tax, or financial advice, and do not replace a qualified employment attorney or HR compliance professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it, and for confirming an employee's full exemption status before classifying them. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The checker this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.
